Denied the usual resources, the analyst enters into his adversary’s spirit, makes it his own, and often perceives immediately the only means—sometimes ludicrously simple—of enticing him into error or hastening him towards a faulty calculation.

Whist has long been celebrated for developing what is called the calculating faculty. Men of the most elevated intellect have displayed a seemingly inexplicable passion for it while dismissing chess as trifling. Certainly no comparable occupation demands so much of the analytical power. Christendom’s finest chess-player may amount to little beyond an excellent player of chess; mastery of whist, however, indicates aptitude for greater enterprises in which one intelligence contends against another. By mastery I mean that perfection of play which comprehends every source of legitimate advantage. These sources are numerous and varied, often hidden in regions of thought beyond the reach of ordinary minds. Close observation produces clear recollection, and in this respect a concentrated chess-player may prosper at whist. Hoyle’s rules, founded simply upon the game’s mechanics, are also generally intelligible enough. A strong memory and strict adherence to “the book” are therefore commonly taken as the whole of sound play. The analyst’s ability, however, reveals itself beyond the confines of mere rules. Silently he gathers a multitude of observations and conclusions. His companions may do likewise; the difference in their resulting knowledge depends less upon the soundness of inference than upon the quality of what is observed. One must know what deserves observation. Our player imposes no narrow bounds upon himself. Although the game is his concern, he refuses no deductions drawn from circumstances outside it. He studies his partner’s face, carefully comparing it with those of his opponents. He considers how each person arranges a hand, frequently identifying trump after trump and honour after honour from the looks cast upon them. Throughout the play he watches every alteration of expression, accumulating information from differing signs of confidence, surprise, satisfaction, and vexation. The way a player collects a trick tells him whether that player can win another in the same suit. He detects a feint from the manner in which the card is laid upon the table. A stray or unguarded remark; a card accidentally dropped or exposed, together with the holder’s concern or indifference about hiding it; the counting of tricks and the sequence in which they are arranged; uneasiness, delay, eagerness, or alarm—all supply his seemingly intuitive understanding with evidence of the actual situation.

With matters so pleasantly and satisfactorily settled, the agreement received solemn confirmation in a further teacup of peppermint mixture, made doubly necessary by the lady’s fluttered and agitated spirits. While they drank it, she informed Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very good,” said he, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll stop at Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send in the morning. Was that what frightened you, my love?”

“Nothing in particular, dear,” she replied evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble persisted. “Won’t you confide in your own B.?”

“Not just now,” said the lady. “Some other day. When we are married, dear.”

“When we are married!” cried Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t insolence from one of those male paupers who—”

“No, no, love!” she interrupted quickly.

“If I believed it was,” Mr. Bumble continued, “if I thought one of them had dared raise his vulgar eyes to that beautiful face—”

“They would never dare, love,” the lady answered.

“They had better not!” exclaimed Mr. Bumble, tightening his fist. “Let me meet any man, whether of this parish or outside it, who would presume upon such a thing, and I promise he would never repeat it!”

Without the embellishment of violent gestures, this might hardly have seemed a lofty tribute to the lady’s attractions. But Mr. Bumble accompanied his threat with such martial flourishes that she was deeply moved by his devotion, and declared admiringly that he was truly a dove.

The dove raised his coat collar and donned his cocked hat. After a long, fond embrace with his future wife, he ventured once more into the cold night wind. He paused only briefly in the male paupers’ ward to abuse its occupants a little, assuring himself that he possessed the bitterness required of a workhouse master. Satisfied with his fitness, he left cheerfully, entertaining radiant expectations of promotion until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper. Noah Claypole, never inclined to exert himself beyond what was needed to eat and drink comfortably, had left the shop open past its usual closing hour. Mr. Bumble struck the counter several times with his cane, without obtaining attention. Seeing a light through the glass window of the small parlour behind the shop, he ventured to look inside and discover what was happening. The discovery surprised him considerably.

On the morning arranged for Admiral and Mrs. Croft to view Kellynch Hall, Anne thought it perfectly natural to take her almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s and stay away until the visit was over. Afterward, she thought it equally natural to regret missing the chance to meet them.

The meeting pleased everyone and settled the whole matter at once. Both ladies had already been inclined to agree, and each therefore found only good manners in the other. As for the gentlemen, the Admiral’s hearty good humor and open, trusting generosity inevitably influenced Sir Walter. Besides, Mr. Shepherd had already flattered him into his finest, most polished behavior by assuring him that the Admiral knew him by reputation as a model of excellent manners.

The house, grounds, and furniture met with approval; so did the Crofts. The terms, the dates, everything and everyone were satisfactory. Mr. Shepherd’s clerks could begin their work without a single preliminary disagreement requiring adjustment in all the provisions of the lease.

Sir Walter immediately pronounced the Admiral the best-looking sailor he had ever met. He even said that, if his own valet could arrange the Admiral’s hair, he would not be embarrassed to appear with him anywhere. In a similarly friendly spirit, the Admiral remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we’d soon strike a bargain, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The baronet won’t set the world on fire, but he seems harmless enough.” Their mutual compliments might have been judged roughly equal.

The Crofts would take possession at Michaelmas. Sir Walter planned to move to Bath during the preceding month, so all the related arrangements needed immediate attention.

Lady Russell was certain Anne would be allowed neither influence nor a useful role in choosing their new house. She disliked the idea of Anne being rushed away so soon and wanted her to remain until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. However, commitments of her own would require Lady Russell to leave Kellynch for several weeks, preventing her from extending the full invitation she wished. Anne dreaded the possible heat of September amid Bath’s glaring white buildings. She also grieved to lose the country’s autumn months, with all their sweet and sorrowful influence. Even so, taking everything into account, she did not think she wanted to stay behind.
